notes: Draft bank for plans/trivia.md. Only status=approved is served. 'match.kind' picks the matcher (boolean | number | text | choice). For number questions 'answer' is the canonical number; for choice questions it is the exact text of the correct choice. 'rejects' are near-misses that must never be accepted, even fuzzily. Sources were checked 2026-11-18. Where sources disagree it is noted and the question is worded around the disagreement. Phase 1 (2026-11-18): every approved question has a 'pool': 'discord' (reserved for the Discord rounds, never served on the web) or 'web' (practice + web daily; also the only pool just-for-fun questions may use). Assigned once, per category sorted by id, every 3rd question -> discord; just-for-fun -> web. Never re-derive it: a question keeps its pool forever.

questions.question: How many bitcoins did Laszlo Hanyecz pay for two pizzas in May 2010?
questions.explanation: 10,000 BTC, paid in a single transaction confirmed on May 22, 2010.

sources.note: Laszlo, May 22 2010: "I just want to report that I successfully traded 10,000 bitcoins for pizza."

questions.question: On what date (month and day) is Bitcoin Pizza Day celebrated every year?
questions.explanation: May 22, the day in 2010 Laszlo reported the pizza trade had gone through.

questions.question: In what year did Laszlo Hanyecz buy two pizzas for 10,000 BTC?
questions.explanation: 2010. The transaction is in block 57,043, mined May 22, 2010.

questions.question: Laszlo's famous photos of the 10,000 BTC pizzas show boxes from which chain?
questions.explanation: Papa John's. Fun wrinkle: in 2016 jercos said he remembered ordering from Domino's, but the photos show Papa John's.

sources.note: Sturdivant ordered two Papa John's pizzas
jercos: "I clearly remember Domino's pizza ... but the pictures show Papa John's."

questions.notes: Sources disagree on the chain: worded around the photos, which every source agrees on.

questions.question: In which US city did Laszlo Hanyecz live when he made the pizza deal?
questions.explanation: Jacksonville, Florida. He posted his location in the thread on May 18, 2010.

questions.question: What was the title of Laszlo's bitcointalk thread offering bitcoin for pizza?
questions.explanation: "Pizza for bitcoins?", started May 18, 2010.

questions.question: True or false: Laszlo wrote that the two pizzas cost only about $25.
questions.explanation: True. June 12, 2010: "the 2 pizzas are only about 25 dollars total, maybe 30 if you give the guy a nice tip."
questions.notes: Popular articles quote $25, $30 or $41. $25-30 is the pizza price Laszlo gave; $41 is what the bitcoin was quoted at. Never ask an exact dollar price as a short answer.

questions.question: According to the Bitcoin Wiki, roughly what were Laszlo's 10,000 BTC worth in US dollars at the time of the offer?
questions.explanation: About $41. Today that much BTC is worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

sources.note: "quoted at $41 at the time of the offer"

questions.question: In which block was the 10,000 BTC pizza transaction confirmed?
The pizza payment was built from many small coins. How many inputs does the 10,000 BTC pizza transaction have?
questions.explanation: 131 inputs, totalling 10,000.99 BTC, mostly from Laszlo's own mining.

questions.question: How much did the 10,000 BTC pizza transaction pay in fees, in BTC?
questions.explanation: 0.99 BTC: inputs of 10,000.99 BTC, one output of exactly 10,000 BTC.

questions.question: True or false: Laszlo baked the pizzas himself and sold them for bitcoin.
questions.explanation: False. Laszlo was the buyer: he paid 10,000 BTC and someone else (jercos) ordered the pizzas for him.
questions.rejectedReason: Snax 2026-11-19: strawman, nobody thinks he baked them
questions.notes: Retired after a Discord report: the premise is a strawman.

questions.question: True or false: the May 22, 2010 pizzas were not Laszlo's only bitcoin pizza purchase that year.
questions.explanation: True. In June he offered 10,000 BTC for two more pizzas "any time", and by August he thanked "everyone who bought me pizza already".
questions.notes: Do NOT ask for his total. Sources disagree (about 80,000 BTC from forum posts; 81,432 BTC of payments; 'closer to 100,000' in a later interview).

questions.question: Laszlo is remembered as an early pioneer of mining bitcoin on what kind of hardware?
questions.explanation: GPUs (graphics cards). On May 10, 2010 he posted about mining on an NVIDIA 8800 GTS.

sources.note: Laszlo says Satoshi had GPU code before him, so ask 'pioneer', not 'inventor'

questions.notes: Never word this as 'invented GPU mining'. Laszlo himself credits Satoshi with having it first.

questions.question: Laszlo published the first Bitcoin client for which operating system?
questions.explanation: Mac OS X, in April 2010. Before that Bitcoin ran on Windows and Linux.

questions.question: In February 2018 Laszlo bought pizza with bitcoin again, this time over which new payment network?
questions.explanation: The Lightning Network (Feb 25, 2018), dubbed "Bitcoin Pizza Day 2".
questions.notes: Sources give the amount as 0.00649 BTC, but only one secondary source was found, so don't ask the amount.

questions.question: Laszlo's first post asked for "maybe 2" pizzas of what size?
questions.explanation: Large: "I'll pay 10,000 bitcoins for a couple of pizzas.. like maybe 2 large ones".

questions.question: True or false: the pizza transaction was mined into a block on the same day Laszlo posted that the trade had succeeded.
questions.explanation: True. Block 57,043 was mined May 22, 2010 (18:16 UTC), the same date as his success post.
questions.notes: Don't ask the time of day: the forum shows times in the viewer's timezone setting, so the post time is ambiguous.

questions.question: Where did Laszlo post his pizza offer?
questions.explanation: The Bitcoin Forum, today's bitcointalk.org (topic 137).

questions.question: What was the forum username of the person who took Laszlo's 10,000 BTC and ordered the pizzas?
questions.explanation: jercos. Laszlo's success post ends with "thanks jercos!"

questions.question: What is the real name of "jercos", who ordered the 10,000 BTC pizzas?
questions.explanation: Jeremy Sturdivant.

questions.question: True or false: jercos paid for the pizzas himself and had them delivered to Laszlo.
questions.explanation: True. The order was paid online with an out-of-state card and delivered to Laszlo in Florida.

sources.note: "ordering two Papa John's pizzas for delivery"
"paid for online with an out of state card"

questions.question: True or false: in a 2016 interview, jercos said he remembered ordering from Domino's, even though the photos show Papa John's.
questions.explanation: True: "I clearly remember Domino's pizza (right down to their particular web interface), but the pictures show Papa John's."

questions.question: True or false: jercos held on to his 10,000 BTC for years.
questions.explanation: False. He said the coins "made it back into the economy fairly quickly, around the time they were worth some $400".

questions.question: Roughly what did jercos say the 10,000 BTC were worth by the time he'd spent them?
questions.explanation: About $400, by his own account in 2016.

sources.note: "around the time they were worth some $400"

questions.notes: Don't ask jercos's age in 2010. Sources say 18 or 19.

questions.question: What is the full title of the Bitcoin whitepaper?
questions.answer: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
aliases: peer to peer electronic cash system
bitcoin a peer to peer electronic cash system
questions.explanation: "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System".

questions.question: On what date did Satoshi announce the Bitcoin whitepaper on the cryptography mailing list?
questions.explanation: October 31, 2008 (Halloween), 18:10 UTC: "Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper".
questions.notes: The mail-archive.com mirror stamps it Sat, 01 Nov 2008 16:16 -0700 (its relay time). The list archive and the Nakamoto Institute say Oct 31. Matching 'november 1' is explicitly rejected; keep the explanation clear.

questions.question: Where did Satoshi first share the Bitcoin whitepaper?
questions.explanation: The Cryptography Mailing List (metzdowd.com). Bitcointalk didn't exist yet.

sources.note: Mailing list: The Cryptography Mailing List

questions.question: How many pages long is the Bitcoin whitepaper, references included?
questions.explanation: Nine pages, in 12 sections.

questions.question: Reference [1] in the Bitcoin whitepaper is a 1998 proposal called "b-money". Who wrote it?
questions.explanation: Wei Dai: "[1] W. Dai, 'b-money', 1998."

questions.question: The whitepaper says Bitcoin's proof-of-work is "similar to" which system by Adam Back?
questions.explanation: Hashcash (reference [6]).

questions.question: True or false: the Bitcoin whitepaper states the 21 million coin limit.
questions.explanation: False. The whitepaper never gives a supply cap. "21,000,000" first appears in Satoshi's v0.1 release email (Jan 2009).

sources.note: Full text contains no supply figure

questions.question: On what date was Bitcoin's genesis block mined?
questions.explanation: January 3, 2009 (block 0, 18:15 UTC).

questions.question: Which newspaper's headline is embedded in Bitcoin's genesis block?
questions.explanation: The Times (London): "The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks".

questions.question: Fill in the blank from the genesis block: "Chancellor on brink of second ____ for banks".
questions.explanation: Bailout.

questions.question: True or false: the 50 BTC reward in the genesis block can be spent.
questions.explanation: False. Because of how the genesis block is coded, its 50 BTC can never be spent.

questions.question: What famous two-word tweet did Hal Finney post in January 2009?
questions.explanation: "Running bitcoin".

sources.note: The tweet (X blocks automated fetches; verified via coverage below)

questions.notes: Date disagreement: most coverage says Jan 10, 2009; the tweet's own timestamp is Jan 11 (timezone). Never ask the date.

questions.question: Who received the first-ever bitcoin transaction from Satoshi?
questions.explanation: Hal Finney, in block 170 on January 12, 2009.

sources.note: First transaction to Finney, 12 Jan 2009, block 170

questions.question: How many BTC did Satoshi send Hal Finney in the first bitcoin transaction?
questions.explanation: 10 BTC (block 170; Satoshi kept 40 BTC as change).

questions.question: Which block contains the first Satoshi-to-Hal Finney transaction?
questions.explanation: Block 170.

questions.question: What version number did Satoshi give the first Bitcoin software release in January 2009?
questions.explanation: v0.1 ("Bitcoin v0.1 released", Jan 9, 2009).

questions.question: Bitcoin v0.1 ran on which operating system only?
questions.explanation: Windows: "Windows only for now."

questions.question: Satoshi's v0.1 release email says total bitcoin circulation will be how many coins?
questions.explanation: 21,000,000 (in practice slightly less: 20,999,999.9769).

questions.question: In what month and year was the bitcoin.org domain registered?
questions.explanation: August 18, 2008, about ten weeks before the whitepaper.

questions.question: In the August 2010 value overflow bug, roughly how many bitcoins were created out of thin air?
questions.explanation: Over 184 billion BTC (184,467,440,737.09551616). The bad block was orphaned and the coins vanished.

sources.note: Two outputs of about 92.2 billion each

questions.notes: Sources disagree on the number of addresses (bitcoin.it: three; Wikipedia: two outputs). Never ask the address count. Number matcher accepts 183.5-185.5 billion.

questions.question: Which block number held the August 2010 value overflow transaction?
questions.explanation: Block 74,638, later replaced on the honest chain.

questions.question: True or false: a fixed Bitcoin client was released within about five hours of the 2010 value overflow bug being found.
questions.explanation: True. The fix shipped within about five hours, and the honest chain overtook the bad one at block 74,691.

sources.note: "within five hours"; good chain overtook at 74691

questions.question: Mt. Gox's name originally stood for "Magic: The Gathering Online ____". Fill in the blank.
questions.explanation: Magic: The Gathering Online eXchange, a trading-card site before it was a bitcoin exchange.

questions.question: Who founded Mt. Gox?
questions.explanation: Jed McCaleb (bitcoin exchange launched July 2010).

questions.question: To whom did Jed McCaleb sell Mt. Gox in March 2011?
questions.explanation: Mark Karpelès, a French developer living in Japan.

questions.question: In what year did Mt. Gox suspend trading and file for bankruptcy?
questions.explanation: 2014 (trading suspended Feb 24; bankruptcy filed in Tokyo Feb 28).

questions.question: At its 2013 peak, roughly what share of the world's bitcoin trades went through Mt. Gox?
questions.explanation: Over 70%.

sources.note: "handling over 70% of the world's bitcoin trades"

questions.question: In what month and year did Satoshi make a last public post on bitcointalk?
questions.explanation: December 12, 2010: "Added some DoS limits, removed safe mode (0.3.19)".
questions.notes: His profile shows him logged in on Dec 13, so ask about the last post, not the last login.

questions.question: Satoshi's last bitcointalk post announced DoS limits in which Bitcoin version?

sources.note: "Added some DoS limits, removed safe mode (0.3.19)"

questions.question: Fill in Satoshi's 2011 email to Mike Hearn: "I've moved on to other ____."
questions.explanation: "things" (April 2011), widely treated as Satoshi's last known message.
questions.notes: Date disagreement: coverage says April 23, 2011, while Wikipedia's infobox ends the active period on April 26, 2011. Never ask the exact day.

questions.question: Complete Satoshi's 2010 quote: "Lost coins only make everyone else's coins worth slightly ____."
questions.explanation: "more. Think of it as a donation to everyone." (bitcointalk, June 21, 2010)

questions.question: True or false: Satoshi Nakamoto's real identity has been confirmed.
questions.explanation: False. "Nakamoto's true identity is unknown."
questions.notes: Time-sensitive in principle. Re-check before each season, and retire it if that ever changes.

questions.question: What email address appears under Satoshi's name on the Bitcoin whitepaper?
questions.explanation: satoshin@gmx.com.

questions.question: True or false: Bitcoin's smallest unit is named after its creator.
questions.explanation: True. 1 satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC.

questions.question: Which bitcointalk user is usually credited with proposing the name "satoshi" for a bitcoin unit?
questions.explanation: ribuck (Nov 2010, at first for 0.01 BTC). Others later pinned it to 0.00000001 BTC.
questions.notes: FLAGGED: attribution is muddy (ribuck coined the name; marcus_of_augustus is credited with today's definition). Secondary sources only.

questions.question: What did a 2014 post on Satoshi's P2P Foundation account say?
questions.explanation: "I am not Dorian Nakamoto." (March 7, 2014)
questions.notes: FLAGGED: I could not verify whether Satoshi wrote this or someone else had the account. Keep the 'account' wording if Snax approves it.

questions.question: Bitcoin's first USD exchange rate (New Liberty Standard, Oct 2009) was about how many BTC per dollar?
questions.explanation: 1,309.03 BTC for $1, based on the electricity cost of mining.
questions.notes: FLAGGED: widely repeated, but Bitbo found no primary source (only period screenshots and forum references).

questions.question: How many BTC did miners earn per block when Bitcoin launched in 2009?
questions.explanation: 50 BTC.

questions.question: Every how many blocks does the bitcoin block subsidy halve?
questions.explanation: Every 210,000 blocks, about every four years.

questions.question: In what year did the first bitcoin halving happen?
questions.explanation: 2012: block 210,000 on November 28, 2012, cut the reward from 50 to 25 BTC.

questions.question: After the April 2024 halving, how many BTC is the block subsidy?
questions.explanation: 3.125 BTC, down from 6.25.
questions.notes: Time-sensitive: true until the next halving (block 1,050,000, about 2028). The plan's season check retires or rewords it then.

questions.question: At what block height did the 2024 halving happen?
questions.explanation: Block 840,000 (April 20, 2024 UTC; still April 19 in the Americas).
questions.notes: Don't ask the date: it's April 19 or 20 depending on timezone.

questions.question: True or false: the 2020 halving cut the block subsidy from 12.5 to 6.25 BTC.
questions.explanation: True (block 630,000, May 11, 2020).

questions.question: Bitcoin's mining difficulty adjusts every how many blocks?
questions.explanation: Every 2,016 blocks (about two weeks).

questions.question: What is Bitcoin's target average time between blocks, in minutes?
questions.explanation: 10 minutes.

questions.question: How many satoshis are in one bitcoin?
Around what year is the last new bitcoin expected to be mined?
questions.explanation: Around 2140 (an estimate: it depends on future block times).

questions.question: Because of rounding, what is the most bitcoin that can ever exist?
questions.explanation: 20,999,999.9769 BTC: rounding at each halving leaves it just under 21 million.

questions.question: True or false: Satoshi said the "bit" in Bitcoin comes from BitTorrent.
questions.explanation: False. Satoshi never explained the name, and nothing links it to BitTorrent. "Bit" is the unit of digital information (binary digit).

sources.note: No etymology or BitTorrent mention in the whitepaper
No etymology in the v0.1 announcement
Shannon 1948: "binary digits, or more briefly bits, a word suggested by J. W. Tukey"

questions.notes: Replaces Snax's suggested "What does the 'bit' in Bitcoin stand for? BitTorrent" (see bt-000 and plans/trivia.md section 3.3).

questions.question: The word "bit", the unit of digital information, is short for what two words?
questions.explanation: Binary digit. Claude Shannon's 1948 paper credits the word to John Tukey.

sources.note: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, 1948

questions.question: What does the 'bit' in Bitcoin stand for?
questions.notes: REJECTED: no source supports it, and it isn't PizzaDAO lore (no repo hits). Kept so it isn't re-added. Use mb-001 / mb-002.

questions.question: True or false: a real email from Satoshi reveals his favorite pizza was pineapple and jalapeño.
questions.explanation: False. In Feb 2024, days after Martti Malmi published his real Satoshi emails, a fake one went viral claiming Satoshi liked pineapple and jalapeños.

sources.note: "a fake email that persuaded most of crypto Twitter that Satoshi liked pineapple and jalapeños on his pizza"
Correction: "This was a meme post and not a true quote."

questions.label: 🍍 Just for fun (crypto-Twitter meme, not history)
questions.question: Just for fun: a fake "Satoshi email" went viral in 2024. What did it claim was Satoshi's favorite slice?
questions.explanation: Pineapple and jalapeño. The email was fake (Fortune, Unchained), but the pizza is great.

sources.note: "meme post and not a true quote"

questions.notes: NEEDS SNAX: his wording "What was Satoshi's favorite slice?" would present a fabricated quote as fact. It isn't PizzaDAO lore either: the repos have no Satoshi link (only a 2025 Catania GPP event titled "Pineapple and jalapenos is a good pizza topping"). Wording above keeps the meme and labels it. 'pineapple' alone is rejected so the answer stays specific; Snax may loosen that.
